predecessors.name: British Empire in India (East India Company rule)
predecessors.text: Company rule in India, the territories of the East India Company taken over by the Crown

predecessors.name: Mughal Empire
predecessors.text: the last Mughal emperor's nominal sovereignty, ended by the Rebellion of 1857

successors.name: Islamic Republic of Pakistan
successors.text: the Dominion of Pakistan, 14 August 1947: West Pakistan and East Pakistan

ledger.x: 1858: the British Crown takes over the government of India from the Company.
ledger.cpn: British Empire in India (East India Company rule)

ledger.x: 1858: the Crown inherits the princely states.
1858: Hyderabad is a princely state under the Crown.
1858: Kashmir and Jammu is a princely state under the Crown.
1860: the western Terai is given to Nepal.
1861: Sikkim becomes a British protectorate.
1864: the Duar War opens.
11 November 1865: the Treaty of Sinchula ends the war.
11 November 1865: British India takes the Bengal Duars and the Kalimpong hills.
11 November 1865: British India takes Dewangiri.
1869: the Nicobar Islands are annexed.
1877: British Baluchistan is formed.
1877: the Khan of Kalat comes under British protection.
1879: the Treaty of Gandamak.
1885: the Third Anglo-Burmese War.
1885: Upper Burma is conquered.
1885: the war ends with Mandalay's fall on 28 November 1885; sporadic resistance continued to 1890 (page).
1888: the Sikkim expedition.
1890: Tibetan claims on Sikkim end.
1891: Hunza and Nagar fall to Anglo-Dogra forces.
31 March 1891: the Anglo-Manipur War opens.
27 April 1891: the British hold Imphal.
27 April 1891: the fighting ends with the fall of Imphal (the expedition 'lasted from 31 March to 27 April 1891'); Tikendrajit and four other commanders were hanged later in 1891.
22 September 1891: the British hand Manipur back to a boy king.
12 November 1893: the Durand Line cedes Asmar and frontier Chitral to Afghanistan.
1895: Chitral comes under the Raj.
9 April 1895: the Nashagam agreement cedes Nasrat and Bashgal to Afghanistan.
December 1903: the British expedition crosses into Tibet.
7 September 1904: the Convention of Lhasa.
September 1904: Britain holds the Chumbi Valley as security.
8 February 1908: Britain leaves the Chumbi Valley.
1911: the capital is to move from Calcutta to Delhi.
March 1914: the McMahon Line puts the tribal tracts of the Assam Himalaya inside the British frontier.
3 July 1914: the Simla accord puts Tawang on the British side of the McMahon Line on paper.
1889: a permanent Political Agent at Gilgit.
1937: Burma leaves British India.
1943: the Andaman and Nicobar Islands are under Japanese occupation.
1944: the Japanese offensive into India.
1944: the offensive is turned back ('mid-1944'); the Burma Campaign continues in Burma, outside the Raj.
1944: British India extends its administration into the Tawang tract south of the Sela Pass.
1945: the Andamans return to the Raj outline (Cliopatria 1945); the Raj page records the Indian National Army surrender 'when Singapore was recaptured in September 1945'.
1947: the Gilgit Agency is handed back.
1947: paramountcy lapses.
1947: Hyderabad is released from paramountcy and 'opted for independence in 1947' (Princely state page); India annexed it a year later.
1947: Kashmir and Jammu is released from paramountcy and 'chose independence' (Partition page); the Instrument of Accession to India followed on 26 October (kashmir-and-jammu dossier).
1947: the British protectorate over Sikkim ends with the Raj ('Protectorate of the British Raj (1861-1947) (de facto)'); 'Sikkim became an Indian protectorate in 1950' (same page).
1947: Hunza and Nagar 'had by then already sent in their accession letters addressed to Muhammad Ali Jinnah' (before 2 November 1947).
1947: 'Swat, Chitral, Dir ... joined Pakistan on independence from the British' (Princely state page).
1947: the Dominion of Pakistan.
1947: the Dominion of India.
15 August 1947: the Raj ends and its claim to Tawang passes to India.
15 August 1947: the Raj's hold on the Tawang tract south of the Sela Pass ends with the Raj; the page says nothing of 1947, and the tract passes to India as part of the inherited boundary.
August 1947: British paramountcy over Kalat lapses with the Raj.

1947: the British Raj ends at midnight on 14-15 August 1947 ('partition took effect 14-15 August 1947 at midnight'); the Indian Independence Act is dated 18 July 1947 and the independence date was announced by Mountbatten on 3 June 1947.

wars.name: Indian Rebellion of 1857
wars.outcome: The rebellion ends in the Crown taking over India in 1858: the Raj page names Rani Lakshmibai, who 'had lost her kingdom by the Doctrine of lapse', and says princes who stayed loyal 'were rewarded with integration into the political system and guaranteed…

wars.name: Duar War
wars.outcome: British victory: the Treaty of Sinchula, 11 November 1865, cedes the Eighteen Duars, the Teesta hill territory and Dewangiri (83 km2); Bhutan receives up to 50,000 rupees a year.

wars.name: Second Anglo-Afghan War
wars.outcome: Treaty of Gandamak, 26 May 1879: Kurram, Pishin, Sibi and the Khyber pass transferred to the British, Afghan foreign policy surrendered; the treaty reaffirmed after Kandahar in 1880.

wars.name: Third Anglo-Burmese War
wars.outcome: British victory in less than two weeks of November 1885: Mandalay entered on 28 November, monarchy abolished, Upper Burma annexed on 1 January 1886.

wars.name: Sikkim expedition of 1888
wars.outcome: 'In 1888 the British sent a military expedition to expel Tibetan forces from Sikkim'; Sikkim remains a British protectorate.

wars.name: Hunza-Nagar Campaign
wars.outcome: Hunza and Nagar 'again subjugated by Anglo-Dogra forces in 1891'.

wars.name: Anglo-Manipur War
wars.outcome: British victory: Imphal taken on 27 April 1891, Tikendrajit hanged, and on 22 September 1891 'the British placed the young boy Meidingngu Churachand on the throne'; Manipur 'was converted into an Indian princely state subject to British Paramountcy'.

wars.name: Chitral rebellion of 1895
wars.outcome: 'Following a rebellion in 1895, Chitral was transferred to the Malakand Agency in the North-West Frontier Province.'

wars.name: British expedition to Tibet
wars.outcome: British victory: Gyantse (April) and Lhasa (August 1904) reached; the Convention of Lhasa of 7 September 1904, revised by the Anglo-Chinese Convention of 1906, with the Chumbi Valley held until the indemnity was paid, to 8 February 1908.

wars.name: Burma campaign
wars.outcome: Japan 'invaded Burma in December 1941' and held much of the colony by the end of 1942; 'In mid-1944, British forces began reversing the Japanese U-Go offensive'; Rangoon 'recaptured in May 1945'.

certainty.note: Frontiers with Afghanistan, Nepal, Bhutan, Tibet and the Burmese hills are approximate; the borders with the princely states are internal.
The Durand Line of 12 November 1893 was demarcated 1894-1896; the north-east frontier (McMahon Line, 1914, surveyed maps from 1937) and the Burma-China frontier stay soft.
The Radcliffe Line, revealed on 17 August 1947.
